previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old female with end-stage renal disease, chronic diastolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and diabetes was admitted due to symptomatic hypotension following hemodialysis. She presented with fatigue and a blood pressure of 62/34 mmHg, requiring fluid resuscitation and placement of a femoral central venous catheter. The hypotension was attributed to excessive fluid removal during dialysis and the cumulative effects of multiple antihypertensive medications. Cardiac biomarkers were elevated, but no acute coronary syndrome was found; findings were consistent with subendocardial ischemia due to low perfusion. Medications were adjusted, including dose reductions in metoprolol and verapamil, and discontinuation of lisinopril, valsartan, and isosorbide mononitrate. Calcium acetate was stopped due to hypophosphatemia. She remained hemodynamically stable, completed dialysis without complications, and was discharged home asymptomatic with updated medication instructions and close follow-up plans.

PROCEDURE: The risks and benefits of the procedure were 
explained to the 
patient and written informed consent was obtained. The patient 
was brought to 
the angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging field. 
The right side 
of the neck and upper chest were prepped and draped in usual 
sterile fashion. 
Access was gained into the right internal jugular vein using 
ultrasound 
guidance and a micropuncture needle. Hard copy ultrasound images 
were 
obtained before and after access. A 0.018 wire was passed into 
the internal 
jugular vein, however, it could not be threaded into the SVC. 5 
cc of 
contrast was administered through the needle and demonstrated 
tight stenosis 
of the distal internal jugular vein near the confluence of the 
subclavian 
vein. Using the venogram, the wire was navigated past the area 
of stenosis and 
into the SVC under fluoroscopic guidance. The needle was removed 
and replaced 
with a micropuncture sheath, through which ___ wire was 
passed into the 
IVC. 
  
At this point, decision was made to dilate the distal internal 
jugular venous 
stenosis. The micropuncture sheath was exchanged for a 6 ___ 
___ 
sheath, with the tip positioned close to the entrance site in 
the internal 
jugular vein. Using an 8-mm ___ balloon, balloon angioplasty 
was performed 
over the area of stenosis in the distal internal jugular vein. 
  
Next, a subcutaneous tunnel was created in the upper chest using 
1% lidocaine 
with epinephrine for anesthesia and a blunt tunneling device. A 
15.5 ___, 
19-cm tip-to-cuff hemodialysis catheter was advanced through the 
tunnel. The 
tract was then dilated and a peel-away sheath was placed over 
the wire. The 
wire is removed and a 15.5 ___ hemodialysis catheter was 
placed through the 
peel-away sheath and positioned with the tip at the level of the 
right atrium. 
The peel-away sheath was removed. The ports were aspirated and 
flushed. 0 
silk was used to suture the catheter in place. ___ Vicryl suture 
was used at 
the puncture site. A sterile dressing was applied. The patient 
tolerated the 
procedure well with no immediate complications. 
  
IMPRESSION: 
  
1. Successful angioplasty of a tight stenosis at the distal 
internal jugular 
vein, near the confluence with the right subclavian vein. 
  
2. Uncomplicated placement of a tunneled 15.5 ___, 19-cm 
tip-to-cuff 
hemodialysis catheter via the right internal jugular vein. The 
tip is in the 
right atrium and the catheter is ready to use.
